unit.title: The Judicial Branch
unit.essential_question: How can unelected judges check the other branches — and what limits their power?

unit.perspectives_title: Who Guards the Constitution? Perspectives on Judicial Power
unit.perspectives_intro: This section weighs the paradox of an unelected branch with the power to overturn the elected ones: a guardian of rights to some, a check that can overreach to others. It is Government Hack–authored instructional synthesis grounded in this unit's sourced record — not a primary source.
perspectives: Because justices are not elected and serve for life, the Court can protect minority rights and the Constitution even when the majority objects (GC.21, GC.22).
Others argue that letting nine unelected judges overturn laws passed by elected representatives is in tension with democracy (GC.21).
Should judges read the Constitution as a 'living document' that adapts, or interpret the 'original intent' of the Framers? The debate shapes every major ruling (GC.22).
Because a justice can serve for decades, the President's nomination and the Senate's confirmation have become high-stakes political battles (GC.20).
unit.tn_connection: Tennessee has sat on the nation's highest bench. John Catron, who had served as Chief Justice of Tennessee's own Supreme Court, was appointed to the U.S. Supreme Court in 1837 and served until his death in Nashville in 1865 — the first Tennessean to help decide what the Constitution means (GC.20).
unit.tn_connection_task: A Tennessean once helped shape the U.S. Supreme Court. Investigate the current Tennessee Supreme Court — name one current justice and one type of case it hears — and record what you find with a source.
unit.belief_check: Predict first: Should nine unelected judges be able to strike down a law passed by Congress and signed by the President? Write your gut answer now — you'll test it against Marbury v. Madison and the idea of judicial review.

play.name: Activist or Restrained?
play.how: 3-minute sorting game (GC.22). Read a short summary of a real ruling and call whether the Court 'made new policy' (judicial activism) or 'deferred to the elected branches / original text' (judicial restraint). Students feel that the same case can look like either, depending on your lens.

GC.19.title: Article III & Judicial Power
GC.19.tn: Analyze Article III of the U.S. Constitution as it relates to judicial power, including the length of terms and the jurisdiction of the U.S. Supreme Court. (—)
GC.19.ican: I can analyze Article III — the judicial power, the tenure of judges, and the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

vocab.def: The authority of a court to hear and decide a case; the Supreme Court has both original and appellate jurisdiction under Article III.
Federal judges hold office 'during good Behaviour' — effectively for life — so they can decide cases free from political pressure.
The authority of a higher court to review and revise the decision of a lower court; most Supreme Court cases arrive this way.

sources.title: U.S. Constitution, Article III, Section 1
sources.quote: The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court… The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour.

sources.title: U.S. Constitution, Article III, Section 2
sources.quote: The judicial Power shall extend to all Cases, in Law and Equity, arising under this Constitution, the Laws of the United States, and Treaties made… under their Authority.

cfu.stem: Why does the Constitution give federal judges their offices 'during good Behaviour' — effectively for life?

options.A: So they can decide cases free from political pressure
options.B: Because judges cannot be removed for any reason
options.C: So the President can replace them every four years
options.D: Because judges must also serve in Congress

cfu.why: DOK 2: Life tenure ('good Behaviour') insulates judges from elections and political retaliation, so they can rule on the law without fear of losing their jobs.

auth.close: Article III creates the judicial branch in a single sentence and leaves the rest to Congress: it vests 'the judicial Power' in 'one supreme Court' and lets Congress create the lower federal courts. To protect judicial independence, judges hold their offices 'during good Behaviour' — effectively for life — and their pay cannot be cut, so they can decide cases without fear of politics. Article III also defines the courts' jurisdiction, the authority to hear a case. The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction (a case starts there) in a few situations, but most cases reach it through appellate jurisdiction — an appeal from a lower court. A federal judge is removed only by impeachment, which is rare. The design trades democratic control for independence: judges answer to the Constitution, not to the voters.
tdq: What does Article III vest in 'one supreme Court,' and who creates the lower courts?
How does 'good Behaviour' tenure protect judicial independence?
What is the difference between original and appellate jurisdiction?

GC.20.title: Selecting & Confirming Justices
GC.20.tn: Explain the processes of selection and confirmation of Supreme Court justices. (—)
GC.20.ican: I can explain how a Supreme Court justice is nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

vocab.def: The President's naming of a person to fill a Supreme Court vacancy; the first step in seating a justice.
The Senate's approval of a nominee by majority vote, after a Judiciary Committee hearing — the 'Advice and Consent' required by the Constitution.
The Senate committee that holds hearings and questions a Supreme Court nominee before the full Senate votes.

sources.title: U.S. Constitution, Article II, Section 2
sources.quote: …he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint… Judges of the supreme Court.

sources.title: U.S. Constitution, Article III, Section 1
sources.quote: …shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour.

cfu.stem: Which two parts of government share the power to seat a new Supreme Court justice?

options.B: The President and the Supreme Court
options.C: The President nominates and the Senate confirms
options.D: The states and the Supreme Court

cfu.why: DOK 2: Article II gives the President the power to nominate and the Senate the power to confirm ('Advice and Consent') — a shared appointment power that checks both branches.

auth.close: No one reaches the Supreme Court alone. When a seat opens, the President nominates a candidate — the first step. The nomination then goes to the Senate, which holds the power of 'Advice and Consent.' The Senate Judiciary Committee holds public hearings, questioning the nominee about their record and judicial philosophy, then recommends the nominee to the full Senate, which confirms by a majority vote. Because a justice serves 'during good Behaviour' — often for decades — a single appointment can shape the law long after the President who made it has left office. That high stakes has turned confirmations into some of the most closely watched political contests in Washington. The process is a deliberate check: the President chooses, but only the Senate can seat.
tdq: What are the two steps to seat a Supreme Court justice, and who controls each?
What does the Senate Judiciary Committee do before the full Senate votes?
Why are confirmations so high-stakes, given how long a justice can serve?

quiz.stem: After the President nominates a Supreme Court justice, who must confirm the nominee?

auth.cer: Claim + Evidence + Reasoning: Should Supreme Court confirmations require a simple majority, or a larger supermajority of the Senate? Defend your claim.

GC.21.title: Judicial Review & Marbury v. Madison
GC.21.tn: Explain the process of judicial review established by Marbury v. Madison. (H, T)
GC.21.ican: I can explain judicial review and how Marbury v. Madison (1803) established it.

vocab.def: The power of the courts to declare a law or government action unconstitutional and therefore void — established by Marbury v. Madison.
Conflicting with the Constitution; a law found unconstitutional cannot be enforced.
A court decision that guides how similar cases are decided in the future; Marbury set the precedent of judicial review.

sources.title: Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137
sources.quote: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.

sources.title: Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137 (holding)
sources.quote: a law repugnant to the constitution is void; and… courts, as well as other departments, are bound by that instrument.

cfu.stem: What power did Marbury v. Madison (1803) establish for the courts?

options.A: The power to elect the President
options.B: Judicial review — the power to declare a law unconstitutional and void

cfu.why: DOK 3: Marshall reasoned that it is 'the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is,' and that a law 'repugnant to the constitution is void' — establishing judicial review.

auth.close: The Constitution never explicitly says the courts can strike down a law — the Supreme Court claimed that power itself, in Marbury v. Madison (1803). In a dispute over a last-minute judicial appointment, Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that when a law conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution must win, because it is the supreme law. 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is,' he wrote, and 'a law repugnant to the constitution is void.' With that, Marshall established judicial review — the power of courts to declare laws and government actions unconstitutional. It made the judiciary a true check on the other branches and set the precedent that still governs how the Court operates. A branch that controls neither the army nor the budget gained the last word on what the Constitution means.
tdq: According to Marshall, whose job is it 'to say what the law is'?
Why does Marshall conclude that a law conflicting with the Constitution must be void?
How did Marbury v. Madison change the power of the judicial branch?

quiz.stem: The 1803 case that established judicial review was:

auth.cer: Claim + Evidence + Reasoning: Was Marshall right to claim the power of judicial review, even though the Constitution does not list it? Defend your claim with evidence from the opinion.

GC.22.title: Deciding What Is Constitutional
GC.22.tn: Describe the Supreme Court's role in determining the constitutionality of laws and acts of the legislative and executive branches. (T)
GC.22.ican: I can describe how the Supreme Court decides the constitutionality of laws and acts, and explain judicial activism and restraint.

vocab.def: An order by which the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case; it takes the 'rule of four' — four of the nine justices — to grant it.
An approach in which judges are more willing to strike down laws or set new policy, often reading the Constitution as a 'living document.'
An approach in which judges defer to the elected branches and to precedent, interpreting the Constitution narrowly by its 'original intent.'

sources.title: Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137
sources.quote: the constitution controls any legislative act repugnant to it.

sources.title: U.S. Constitution, Article VI (Supremacy Clause)
sources.quote: This Constitution… shall be the supreme Law of the Land; and the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby.

cfu.stem: How do judicial activism and judicial restraint differ?

options.A: Activism means judges never rule; restraint means they rule on everything
options.B: Activism applies only to state courts; restraint only to federal courts
options.C: They are two names for the same approach
options.D: Activism is a greater willingness to strike down laws or set new policy; restraint defers to the elected branches and precedent

cfu.why: DOK 3: Judicial activism describes judges more willing to overturn laws or make new policy (often via a 'living Constitution'); judicial restraint describes judges who defer to elected branches and original intent.

auth.close: Because Marbury established judicial review, the Supreme Court is the final judge of whether a law or executive act is constitutional. Getting there is selective: after losing in lower courts, a party petitions for a writ of certiorari, and it takes the 'rule of four' — four of the nine justices — for the Court to take the case. When the Court rules, it does not just settle that dispute; it sets precedent for the whole country. How boldly the Court should use this power is contested. Judges who practice judicial activism are more willing to strike down laws or set new policy, often treating the Constitution as a 'living document' that adapts to the times. Judges who practice judicial restraint defer to the elected branches and to precedent, reading the Constitution by its 'original intent.' The Warren, Burger, Rehnquist, and Roberts Courts are often placed along this spectrum. As Marshall put it, 'the constitution controls any legislative act repugnant to it' — but reasonable people still argue over what the Constitution requires.
tdq: How does a case actually reach the Supreme Court (cert and the 'rule of four')?
Contrast judicial activism and judicial restraint using an example of each.
How does the Supremacy Clause support the Court's power to strike down conflicting laws?
